name: Canada (Federal, Ontario, British Columbia)
summary: Employment law in Canada is mostly provincial: the Toronto office is governed by Ontario's Employment Standards Act, 2000 (ESA), OHSA and Human Rights Code, and Vancouver/Burnaby by BC's Employment Standards Act, WorkSafeBC rules and Human Rights Code. Federal law covers payroll (CPP/CPP2, EI, income tax), immigration, competition law and privacy for commercial data. There is no at-will employment. Unless a written termination clause is enforceable, employees are owed common-law reasonable notice (Bardal factors, often up to about 24 months), which dwarfs the statutory minimums and is the biggest termination cost. Ontario legislates almost every year (Working for Workers Acts 2021-2025; job-posting pay ranges and AI disclosure since Jan 1, 2026). BC requires gender pay-gap reports from employers with 50+ BC employees by Nov 1, 2026. Common mistakes by US-HQ employers: at-will or US-template offer letters, non-competes (void in Ontario), equity forfeiture language that fails Matthews v. Ocean Nutrition, and one 'Canada' policy set that ignores Ontario/BC differences and Quebec.

ratingNotes.termination: No cause is needed to terminate, but common-law notice (up to ~24 months), strict termination-clause case law (Waksdale, Dufault, Baker 2026) and Ontario ESA severance based on global payroll make exits expensive.
ratingNotes.representation: No works councils, and unions are rare in private tech. The main mandatory bodies are joint health & safety committees (20+ workers); BC allows single-step card-check union certification.
ratingNotes.privacy: BC PIPA covers employee data. In Ontario, employee data of provincially regulated employers is covered by no private-sector statute (only common law and the ESA e-monitoring policy). Quebec Law 25 is strict, and federal reform (Bill C-36) is pending.
ratingNotes.payTransparency: Ontario: pay ranges, AI disclosure and applicant follow-up in postings since Jan 2026, plus the Pay Equity Act. BC: pay ranges, a ban on asking pay history, and public gender pay-gap reports (50+ employees from 2026).
ratingNotes.workingTime: ON IT professionals and BC 'high technology professionals' are largely exempt from hours/overtime rules. The main obligations are policies (e.g., ON disconnecting-from-work policy) and records.
ratingNotes.leave: Long job-protected leaves (parental up to ~18 months, 27-week illness leaves in ON and BC) are funded mainly by EI. Employer-paid statutory leave is limited (BC 5 paid sick days; 5 paid domestic-violence days).
ratingNotes.immigration: Fast routes still exist for engineers (Global Talent Stream, ICT, CUSMA), but temporary-resident cuts, spousal work permit limits and PGWP changes in 2024-2026 narrowed the options.
ratingNotes.changeVelocity: Ontario passes a Working for Workers Act almost every year. BC amended its ESA three times in 2025-2026. Federal privacy reform (Bill C-36) and immigration levels keep changing.

keyFacts.label: Employment model
keyFacts.value: No at-will employment. Indefinite-term employment is the norm. An employer may dismiss without cause only by giving ESA minimum notice/pay plus common-law reasonable notice, unless an enforceable written clause limits entitlement to ESA minimums. Provincially regulated tech employers follow the ON ESA 2000 and BC ESA; the Canada Labour Code applies only to federally regulated sectors (banks, telecom, interprovincial transport).

keyFacts.label: Contracts & offer letters
keyFacts.value: A written contract is not legally required but is essential: termination, IP and confidentiality clauses must be signed before the start date, or new consideration is needed. In ON, employers with 25+ employees must give new hires written information (legal/operating name, contact details, work location, starting pay, pay period/payday, anticipated hours) before the first day, since July 1, 2025. Quebec hires need a French contract.

keyFacts.label: Probation
keyFacts.value: No statutory probation. ON ESA notice and BC compensation for length of service (CLOS) start only after 3 months' service. A contractual probation clause must clearly limit notice, or common-law reasonable notice still applies. Assess suitability in good faith and document it.

keyFacts.label: Notice (employer)
keyFacts.value: ON ESA: 1 week (<1 yr), 2 weeks (1-3 yrs), then 1 week per year up to 8 weeks. BC CLOS: 1 week after 3 months, 2 weeks after 12 months, 3 weeks after 3 years plus 1 week per extra year up to 8 weeks. Common law (if no enforceable clause) applies the Bardal factors (age, service, role, availability of similar work): often ~3-24 months for professionals, with 24 months a soft cap.

keyFacts.label: Notice (employee)
keyFacts.value: ON and BC ESAs require no resignation notice. Exception in ON: employees who resign after receiving mass-termination notice must give 1 week (<2 yrs) or 2 weeks. At common law employees owe reasonable notice, typically 2-4 weeks (longer for key roles), and damages are rarely pursued. Contracts usually set 2-4 weeks.

keyFacts.label: Statutory severance
keyFacts.value: ON ESA severance pay is separate from notice: 1 week per year of service (pro-rated), max 26 weeks. It applies after 5+ years' service when the employer's global payroll is C$2.5M+ (always met here). BC has no separate severance, but BC group-termination notice is added on top of individual CLOS. The real exposure is common-law damages: salary, bonus, benefits and equity for the full notice period.

keyFacts.label: Working hours & overtime
keyFacts.value: ON: max 8 h/day (or the regular day) and 48 h/week unless agreed in writing; overtime at 1.5x after 44 h/week. BC: 1.5x after 8 h/day or 40 h/week, 2x after 12 h/day. ON IT professionals and BC 'high technology professionals' (ESR s.37.8) are exempt from hours/overtime rules; the BC exemption also covers statutory holidays. Confirm role by role, because technicians and support staff may not qualify.

keyFacts.label: Minimum wage
keyFacts.value: ON: C$17.60/h, rising to C$17.95 on Oct 1, 2026 (student rate C$16.90); indexed to CPI each Oct 1. BC: C$18.25/h since June 1, 2026; indexed each June 1. Mainly relevant to interns/co-ops and to salary floors for exempt roles.

keyFacts.label: Annual leave
keyFacts.value: ON: 2 weeks plus 4% vacation pay; 3 weeks plus 6% after 5 years. BC: 2 weeks (4%) after 12 months; 3 weeks (6%) after 5 years; must be taken within 12 months of being earned. Vacation pay is calculated on most wages, including non-discretionary bonuses. Tech market practice is 3-4 weeks plus personal/floater days.

keyFacts.label: Public holidays
keyFacts.value: ON (9): New Year's, Family Day, Good Friday, Victoria Day, Canada Day, Labour Day, Thanksgiving, Christmas, Boxing Day (Civic Holiday and Easter Monday are not statutory). BC (11): New Year's, Family Day, Good Friday, Victoria Day, Canada Day, BC Day, Labour Day, National Day for Truth and Reconciliation (Sept 30), Thanksgiving, Remembrance Day, Christmas (Boxing Day is not statutory).

keyFacts.label: Sick leave
keyFacts.value: ON: 3 unpaid days/yr after 2 weeks' service; employers may not require a medical note for these days (since Oct 28, 2024). ON also has a 27-week unpaid long-term illness leave (since June 19, 2025). BC: 5 paid plus 3 unpaid days after 90 days; no sick notes for absences of up to 5 consecutive days for the first 2 absences each calendar year (since Nov 12, 2025); 27-week serious illness/injury leave (since Nov 28, 2025).

keyFacts.label: Parental leave
keyFacts.value: Unpaid job-protected leave: pregnancy 17 weeks (ON and BC); parental up to 61 weeks after pregnancy leave (63 in ON / 62 in BC for other parents). Income comes from federal EI: 55% of insurable earnings (about C$729/week max in 2026) for 35 standard weeks, or 33% for 61 extended weeks, plus shared-parental weeks. Tech market practice: top-up to 80-100% for roughly 15-26 weeks through a registered SUB plan.

keyFacts.label: Social insurance / mandatory benefits
keyFacts.value: 2026 figures: CPP 5.95% each (employee and employer) on earnings C$3,500-74,600 (max C$4,230.45 each); CPP2 4% each on C$74,600-85,000 (max C$416); EI 1.63% employee and 2.282% employer (1.4x) on up to C$68,900 (max C$1,123.07 / C$1,572.30). Provincial costs: ON Employer Health Tax and WSIB; BC Employer Health Tax and WorkSafeBC (EHT 1.95% of payroll at scale; verify thresholds). OHIP and BC MSP (premiums abolished in 2020) are tax-funded.

keyFacts.label: Payroll frequency & final pay
keyFacts.value: ON: a regular recurring payday (bi-weekly or semi-monthly is common), with direct deposit to an account the employee chooses. BC: at least semi-monthly, paid within 8 days after the pay period ends. Final pay: ON by the later of 7 days after termination or the next regular payday. BC within 48 hours if the employer terminates, or 6 days if the employee quits.

keyFacts.label: Employee representation
keyFacts.value: No works councils or mandatory consultation outside unionized workplaces; unions are rare in private tech. Certification is under the ON Labour Relations Act and the BC Labour Relations Code; BC has single-step card-check. Mandatory joint health & safety committee at 20+ workers (ON JHSC, BC JOHSC); a health & safety representative is required at 6-19 workers (ON) or 10-19 (BC).

keyFacts.label: Data privacy law
keyFacts.value: ON: no private-sector statute covers employee data of provincially regulated employers (PIPEDA covers only commercial activity). The common law (intrusion upon seclusion), the ESA electronic-monitoring policy and contracts govern. BC: PIPA covers employee personal information, which may be collected without consent if reasonable for the employment relationship, with notice. Quebec: Law 25. Federal Bill C-27 died in Jan 2025; its replacement, Bill C-36 (Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act), was tabled June 15, 2026.

keyFacts.label: Record retention
keyFacts.value: CRA payroll/tax records: 6 years from the end of the tax year to which they relate; ROE-related records: 6 years. ON ESA: employee and wage records 3 years; job postings, application forms and interview-outcome notices 3 years; disconnecting and e-monitoring policies 3 years after they cease to apply. BC ESA payroll records: 4 years after employment ends (verify). Foreign-worker (IRCC/ESDC) documents: 6 years.

keyFacts.label: Non-competes & IP
keyFacts.value: ON bans employee non-competes (ESA s.67.2, agreements on or after Oct 25, 2021), except on the sale of a business and for C-suite executives. BC has no ban, but courts rarely enforce employee non-competes (Shafron v. KRG, SCC 2009: must be reasonable and unambiguous; no blue-pencilling). Narrow non-solicits and confidentiality clauses remain usable. There is no statutory employee-invention assignment, so use an express assignment plus a moral-rights waiver.

keyFacts.label: Language requirements
keyFacts.value: ON and BC: English is fine for contracts, policies and postings. Quebec (caution for remote hires): under the Charter of the French Language as amended by Bill 96, employment contracts, policies, job postings and written communications must be in French, and requiring English needs justification. Businesses with 25+ Quebec employees must register with the OQLF (since June 1, 2025).

keyFacts.label: Regulator(s)
keyFacts.value: ON: Ministry of Labour, Immigration, Training and Skills Development (ESA/OHSA), Pay Equity Office, Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario, WSIB, Accessibility Directorate. BC: Employment Standards Branch, WorkSafeBC, BC Human Rights Tribunal, Ministry of Finance (pay transparency), OIPC BC. Federal: CRA, ESDC/Service Canada (ROE, LMIA), IRCC, Competition Bureau, Office of the Privacy Commissioner.

mandatoryPolicies.name: Disconnecting from work policy (ON)
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: Employers with 25+ Ontario employees on Jan 1 need a written policy by March 1 of that year, with the preparation date and dates of any changes. Give a copy to employees within 30 days (and to new hires within 30 days of hire). Keep for 3 years after it ceases to apply. The policy does not create a right to disconnect.
mandatoryPolicies.source: ON ESA 2000, Part VII.0.1 (Working for Workers Act, 2021)

mandatoryPolicies.name: Electronic monitoring policy (ON)
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: Same 25+ employee / March 1 trigger. The policy must state whether the employer monitors electronically and, if so, how, in what circumstances and for what purposes. Copies go to employees within 30 days; retain for 3 years. The policy creates no new privacy right.
mandatoryPolicies.source: ON ESA 2000, Part XI.1 (Working for Workers Act, 2022)

mandatoryPolicies.name: Workplace violence policy and program (ON)
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: Written policy, posted where there are 6+ workers, reviewed at least annually. The program must include a risk assessment and measures and procedures for summoning help, reporting and investigation. Also covers domestic violence that may occur in the workplace.

mandatoryPolicies.name: Workplace harassment policy and program (ON)
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: Written policy (posted at 6+ workers) and a program developed with the JHSC/representative. It must cover reporting (including an alternative channel when the supervisor is involved), investigation, confidentiality, and informing the parties in writing of results and corrective action. Covers sexual and, since Oct 2024, virtual harassment. Review at least annually.
mandatoryPolicies.source: ON OHSA ss. 32.0.6-32.0.8 (as amended by Working for Workers Five Act, 2024)

mandatoryPolicies.name: Occupational health & safety policy (ON)
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: Written health and safety policy and a program to implement it. Review at least annually and post it where there are 6+ workers. Also post the OHSA and the 'Prevention Starts Here' poster.

mandatoryPolicies.name: AODA accessibility policies, plan, training and report (ON)
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: Accessibility policies (documented if 50+ employees), a multi-year accessibility plan (50+), and training on the IASR and Human Rights Code for all staff. Requirements include accessible recruitment notices, individual accommodation plans and a return-to-work process (50+), workplace emergency response information, and WCAG 2.0 AA public websites (50+). File an accessibility compliance report every 3 years if 20+ employees (next due Dec 31, 2026).
mandatoryPolicies.source: Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act, 2005; O. Reg. 191/11 (IASR)

mandatoryPolicies.name: Job posting compliance procedure (ON)
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: Applies to employers with 25+ employees for publicly advertised postings since Jan 1, 2026. Postings must show expected pay or a range (spread of max C$50,000; exempt if the pay exceeds C$200,000/yr), disclose AI use in screening, assessment or selection, state whether an existing vacancy exists, and not require Canadian experience. Tell interviewed applicants the outcome within 45 days of the last interview. Keep records 3 years.
mandatoryPolicies.source: ON ESA 2000, job posting provisions added by Working for Workers Four and Five Acts, 2024, and regulations

mandatoryPolicies.name: Pay equity (ON)
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: Employers with 10+ employees in Ontario must establish and maintain pay equity between female and male job classes of equal or comparable value (job-to-job or proportional comparison). Re-check after reorganizations or when new job classes are created.

mandatoryPolicies.name: Bullying and harassment policy and procedures (BC)
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: The policy must state that bullying and harassment is not acceptable. Procedures must cover reporting and how the employer investigates and responds, with a reasonable response aimed at fully addressing the incident. Inform and train workers and supervisors, and review the policy and procedures annually.
mandatoryPolicies.source: BC Workers Compensation Act (general duties); WorkSafeBC OHS Policies D3-115-2 and related (verify numbering)

mandatoryPolicies.name: Occupational health & safety program (BC)
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: A formal written OHS program is required for 50+ workers, or 20+ where there is at least moderate hazard (e.g., labs). Also required: a joint committee (JOHSC) at 20+ workers, a worker representative at 10-19, orientation for new and young workers, a first-aid assessment and a working-alone procedure.
mandatoryPolicies.source: BC OHS Regulation Part 3 (s.3.1, s.3.23) and Workers Compensation Act Part 2

mandatoryPolicies.name: Pay transparency compliance (BC)
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: Every public posting must show the expected pay or pay range (since Nov 1, 2023). Applicants may not be asked for pay history (since May 11, 2023), and employees may not face reprisal for discussing pay. Employers with 50+ BC employees (counted as at Jan 1, 2026) must publish a pay transparency report by Nov 1, 2026, and annually after that.
mandatoryPolicies.source: BC Pay Transparency Act (SBC 2023) and Pay Transparency Regulation

mandatoryPolicies.name: Privacy policies and privacy officer (BC; ON best practice)
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: BC PIPA requires designating a person responsible for compliance, developing policies and practices, a complaint process, and notice of purposes when collecting employee personal information. In ON, this is expected practice and supports the e-monitoring policy.
mandatoryPolicies.source: BC Personal Information Protection Act ss.4-5, 13-16

mandatoryPolicies.name: Human rights, accommodation and anti-discrimination policy
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: The duty to accommodate (disability, family status, creed, etc.) to the point of undue hardship applies everywhere. A written policy and accommodation process is the expected way to show compliance, including accommodation in recruitment under AODA.
mandatoryPolicies.source: Ontario Human Rights Code; BC Human Rights Code

mandatoryPolicies.name: Antitrust in HR (no-poach / wage-fixing) policy
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: Since June 23, 2023, agreements between unaffiliated employers to fix wages or terms, or not to solicit or hire each other's employees, are criminal offences (up to 14 years and discretionary fines). HR benchmarking and salary-survey data sharing must go through safe channels.
mandatoryPolicies.source: Competition Act s.45(1.1); Competition Bureau enforcement guidelines

mandatoryPolicies.name: Foreign worker compliance program
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: Employers of work-permit holders must meet the offer terms (wages, duties, conditions), keep supporting documents for 6 years, and cooperate with IRCC/ESDC inspections. For LMIA-exempt hires, submit the offer through the IRCC Employer Portal and pay the compliance fee.
mandatoryPolicies.source: Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations ss.209.2-209.4 (TFWP) and ss.209.11-209.12 (IMP) (verify section references)

mandatoryPolicies.name: Employment standards information and posters (ON)
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: Post the current ESA poster ('Employment Standards in Ontario') and give each employee a copy within 30 days of hire. Employers with 25+ employees must also provide the written new-hire information statement.
mandatoryPolicies.source: ON ESA 2000 s.2 and new-employee information provisions (in force July 1, 2025)

mandatoryPolicies.name: Psychological harassment policy (Quebec, only if Quebec employees)
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: Any Quebec-based employee (including remote) triggers a written psychological and sexual harassment prevention and complaint-handling policy in French, plus French-language employment documents.
mandatoryPolicies.source: Quebec Act respecting labour standards s.81.19; Charter of the French Language

mandatoryPolicies.name: Federal Contractors Program employment equity (conditional)
mandatoryPolicies.requirement: Applies if the Canadian entity has 100+ employees and receives a Government of Canada goods/services contract of C$1M+. The employer must certify and implement employment equity (workforce analysis, goals).
mandatoryPolicies.source: Federal Contractors Program (ESDC) under the Employment Equity Act framework (verify thresholds)

hiring.req: Ontario job-posting content (25+ employees, since Jan 1, 2026)
hiring.detail: Configure the ATS so Ontario public postings show a pay figure or range with a spread of no more than C$50,000 (roles over C$200,000/yr are exempt). Also state whether the vacancy currently exists and disclose any AI used to screen, assess or select applicants. Remove any 'Canadian experience' requirement from postings and application forms. Internal-only postings and general 'help wanted' campaigns are excluded.
hiring.cite: ON ESA 2000 job posting provisions (Working for Workers Four and Five Acts, 2024)

hiring.req: Ontario applicant follow-up and record keeping
hiring.detail: Tell every interviewed applicant within 45 days of their last interview whether a hiring decision was made (in person, in writing or by email/ATS). Keep the posting, application form and notices for 3 years.

hiring.req: BC pay range and pay-history ban
hiring.detail: Every public BC posting must include the expected pay or pay range (since Nov 1, 2023). Remove 'current/expected salary history' fields from BC application flows and recruiter scripts; asking about expectations is allowed, asking about history is not. Do not penalize pay discussions.

Do not ask about protected grounds (age, disability, family status, place of origin; in ON also citizenship and record of offences). Criminal and credit checks need a legitimate job requirement and consent; in ON, give notice under the Consumer Reporting Act. Offer accommodation in recruitment (AODA).
hiring.cite: ON Human Rights Code; BC Human Rights Code s.13; AODA IASR s.22-23

hiring.req: Canada-specific offer letter signed before start
hiring.detail: Use a Canadian contract with an ESA-compliant termination clause, no Ontario non-compete, IP assignment and moral-rights waiver, and equity language covering the notice period. It must be signed before the employee starts; later changes need new consideration.
hiring.cite: Waksdale v. Swegon (2020 ONCA 391); Baker v. Van Dolder's Home Team (2026 ONCA 568); ESA s.67.2

hiring.detail: Use the fastest route that fits. Intra-company transfer: LMIA-exempt, for managers or specialized-knowledge staff with 1 year at a related entity in the last 3. CUSMA Professional: US/Mexican engineers and computer systems analysts; US citizens can apply at the port of entry. Global Talent Stream LMIA: Category B includes software and computer engineers; 10-business-day LMIA standard, 2-week work permit, Labour Market Benefits Plan required. A regular high-wage LMIA takes about 90 days (Aug 2026).
hiring.cite: IRPR s.205(a), R204 (CUSMA); ESDC Global Talent Stream

hiring.detail: Planned temporary-worker arrivals fall from 367,750 (2025) to 230,000 (2026-28), with a target of temporary residents below 5% of the population by end-2027. The high-wage LMIA threshold rose 20% (Nov 2024). Low-wage LMIAs are refused in areas with 6%+ unemployment. Express Entry arranged-employment points were removed in 2025 (verify). Budget 2025 promised an H-1B pathway; IRCC consulted in Aug-Sep 2026 on an H-1B Express Entry category for 2027.
hiring.cite: IRCC 2026-2028 Immigration Levels Plan; ESDC TFWP program notices

hiring.detail: Since Jan 21, 2025, spousal open work permits are limited to spouses of workers in TEER 0/1 (or listed TEER 2/3) jobs with 16+ months left on their permit, and dependent children no longer qualify. PGWPs cannot be extended, so start LMIA or PR planning early. Students who applied on or after Nov 1, 2024 face language tests (CLB 7 for degree holders) and field-of-study rules for non-degree programs.
hiring.cite: IRCC notice on family open work permits (Jan 2025); IRCC PGWP eligibility

hiring.detail: For LMIA-exempt hires, submit the offer of employment in the IRCC Employer Portal and pay the C$230 compliance fee. Keep wages and duties consistent with the permit, keep records 6 years, and diarize permit expiries (a SIN starting with 9 expires with the permit).

Do not let hiring managers hire 'remote anywhere in Canada' without legal review. Quebec needs French postings, contracts and policies, OQLF registration at 25+ employees, and Law 25 compliance. An employee with 2+ years' service can seek reinstatement for dismissal without good and sufficient cause.
hiring.cite: Charter of the French Language (Bill 96); Act respecting labour standards s.124; Law 25

onboarding.detail: Before day one, where practicable, give: legal and operating name, contact details, work location, starting pay, pay period and payday, and a general description of anticipated hours. Build it into the offer packet.

onboarding.req: ON ESA poster and policies within 30 days
onboarding.detail: Give the current ESA poster, the disconnecting-from-work policy and the electronic-monitoring policy within 30 days of hire, and post the ESA poster at the workplace.
onboarding.cite: ON ESA s.2; Parts VII.0.1 and XI.1

onboarding.detail: ON: mandatory basic OHS awareness training for workers and supervisors, plus information on violence and harassment programs. BC: new and young worker orientation before starting work, covering bullying and harassment procedures, first aid and emergency procedures.
onboarding.cite: ON O. Reg. 297/13; OHSA s.32.0.5; BC OHS Regulation s.3.23

onboarding.detail: Train every Ontario employee on the IASR and the Human Rights Code as it relates to disability, as soon as practicable, and keep training records.

Collect the SIN (the employee must provide it within 3 days of starting), TD1 federal plus TD1ON/TD1BC, and direct-deposit details for an account of the employee's choice. Record work-permit expiry for 9-series SINs.
onboarding.cite: Employment Insurance Regulations; Income Tax Act; ON ESA s.11 (direct deposit, June 2024)

onboarding.detail: Execute the invention assignment, prior-inventions schedule, moral-rights waiver and confidentiality agreement before access is granted. Screen for US EAR deemed-reexport licensing before giving third-country nationals controlled technology.
onboarding.cite: Copyright Act ss.13(3), 14.1; US EAR 15 CFR 734.14

onboarding.detail: Enrol the hire in group benefits on day one (market practice). Relocating hires face a BC MSP waiting period (the rest of the arrival month plus 2 months), so provide interim private coverage. OHIP has no waiting period (verify for the individual's status).
onboarding.cite: BC Medicare Protection Act; OHIP eligibility rules

payAndPayroll.detail: Register a CRA payroll (RP) account. Withhold federal and provincial income tax, CPP/CPP2 and EI, and remit on the remitter schedule; large employers are accelerated remitters (up to 4 times a month). Late remittance draws 10% penalties plus interest.
payAndPayroll.cite: Income Tax Act s.153; CPP Act; EI Act

payAndPayroll.detail: CPP 5.95% each on C$3,500-74,600 (max C$4,230.45); CPP2 4% each on C$74,600-85,000 (max C$416); EI 1.63% employee and 2.282% employer on up to C$68,900. Quebec employees use QPP and QPIP instead, with a lower EI rate (1.30%).
payAndPayroll.cite: CRA CPP and EI rate tables 2026

payAndPayroll.req: Provincial payroll taxes and workers' compensation
payAndPayroll.detail: ON Employer Health Tax and BC Employer Health Tax (1.95% of payroll for large employers; verify exemptions). WSIB (ON) and WorkSafeBC premiums at the office/tech rate group; report payroll annually.
payAndPayroll.cite: ON Employer Health Tax Act; BC Employer Health Tax Act; WSIA; BC Workers Compensation Act

payAndPayroll.detail: ON: pay on a regular recurring payday with an itemized wage statement each payday. BC: pay at least semi-monthly, within 8 days after each pay period ends, with a written wage statement. Deductions from wages need written authorization and statutory permission.
payAndPayroll.cite: ON ESA ss.11-13; BC ESA ss.17, 21, 22, 27

payAndPayroll.detail: 4% (6% after 5 years) of vacationable wages, including non-discretionary bonuses and commissions. In ON, paying vacation pay on each pay cheque requires a written agreement (since June 21, 2024). Pay out accrued vacation pay at termination.
payAndPayroll.cite: ON ESA ss.35.2-36; BC ESA ss.57-58

payAndPayroll.detail: ON: equal pay for substantially the same work regardless of sex (ESA s.42), plus the Pay Equity Act for employers with 10+ employees. BC: anti-reprisal for pay discussions and annual gender pay-gap reporting (Pay Transparency Act). Audit pay ranges before BC reports are published.
payAndPayroll.cite: ON ESA s.42; Ontario Pay Equity Act; BC Pay Transparency Act

payAndPayroll.detail: RSUs are employment income at vesting; stock options are taxed at exercise. The 50% stock option deduction is capped at C$200,000 of annual vesting value for non-CCPC employers with more than C$500M consolidated revenue. Withhold on equity income and report it on the T4 with the correct codes. ESPP discounts are taxable.

Issue T4 slips (employees) and T4A slips (contractors, other payments), and file them with the summary by the last day of February. Electronic filing is mandatory above 5 slips. Quebec employees also need RL-1 slips.

timeAndLeave.detail: Classify each role. ON IT professionals and managers, and BC high-technology professionals (ESR s.37.8), are exempt from hours and overtime rules. Lab technicians, test operators and admin staff usually are not: ON overtime at 1.5x after 44 h/week; BC at 1.5x after 8 h/day or 40 h/week and 2x after 12 h/day.
timeAndLeave.cite: ON ESA Parts VII-VIII and O. Reg. 285/01; BC ESA Part 4; BC ESR s.37.8

timeAndLeave.detail: ON: 2 weeks (3 after 5 years) per vacation entitlement year, taken within 10 months. BC: 2 weeks after 12 months (3 after 5 years), taken within 12 months. Policies may give more but not less; 'unlimited PTO' must still track the statutory minimum and vacation pay.
timeAndLeave.cite: ON ESA Part XI; BC ESA Part 7

timeAndLeave.detail: ON has 9 public holidays and BC 11 (BC includes Sept 30, Remembrance Day and BC Day; ON includes Boxing Day). BC: to qualify for holiday pay, an employee must be employed 30 days and have worked or earned wages on 15 of the last 30 days; work on the holiday is paid at 1.5x plus an average day's pay. BC high-tech professionals are exempt from BC Part 5.
timeAndLeave.cite: ON ESA Part X; BC ESA Part 5

timeAndLeave.detail: ON: 3 unpaid days; no medical note can be required for them (since Oct 28, 2024), though other evidence reasonable in the circumstances may be requested. BC: 5 paid plus 3 unpaid days after 90 days; no sick note for absences of up to 5 consecutive days for the first 2 absences each calendar year (since Nov 12, 2025). Fitness-to-return and accommodation information may still be requested.
timeAndLeave.cite: ON ESA s.50.0.1; BC ESA s.49.1 and s.49.2 (Bill 11, 2025)

timeAndLeave.req: Other ON ESA leaves (unpaid unless noted)
timeAndLeave.detail: Family responsibility 3 days, bereavement 2 days, family caregiver 8 weeks, critical illness 17/37 weeks, family medical 28 weeks, and domestic/sexual violence 5 paid + 5 unpaid days + 15 weeks. Also long-term illness 27 weeks (June 2025), organ donor, reservist, child death 104 weeks, and 3-day job-seeking leave in mass terminations (Nov 27, 2025). A 16-week placement-of-child leave is enacted but not yet in force.
timeAndLeave.cite: ON ESA Part XIV; Working for Workers Six and Seven Acts

timeAndLeave.detail: Family responsibility 5 days, bereavement 3 days, compassionate care 27 weeks, critical illness 16/36 weeks, and domestic/sexual violence 5 paid + 5 unpaid days + up to 15 weeks. Also serious personal illness or injury 27 weeks (Nov 28, 2025), jury duty, reservist, and child death 104 weeks.

timeAndLeave.req: Pregnancy and parental leave with EI
timeAndLeave.detail: Pregnancy leave is 17 weeks; parental leave is up to 61-63 weeks. Continue benefit plan contributions during leave unless the employee opts out, and reinstate the employee to the same or a comparable job. To top up EI without reducing benefits, register a Supplemental Unemployment Benefit (SUB) plan with Service Canada.
timeAndLeave.cite: ON ESA ss.46-53; BC ESA ss.50-56; EI Regulations (SUB plans)

timeAndLeave.req: Disconnecting from work and hybrid work
timeAndLeave.detail: Keep the ON disconnecting policy current. A remote arrangement written into the contract can make a return-to-office mandate a constructive dismissal risk, so document hybrid arrangements as policy-based and revocable.
timeAndLeave.cite: ON ESA Part VII.0.1; common law (constructive dismissal)

timeAndLeave.req: Benefit continuation and job protection during leave
timeAndLeave.detail: Seniority and service keep accruing during statutory leaves in ON and BC. Dismissing an employee during or right after a protected leave creates reprisal and human rights exposure. Document legitimate business reasons (e.g., a reorganization decided before the leave).
timeAndLeave.cite: ON ESA s.51, s.74; BC ESA s.54, s.56

benefits.detail: OHIP (ON) and MSP (BC; premiums abolished Jan 1, 2020) cover physician and hospital care with no employee premium; Ontario collects the Ontario Health Premium through income tax withholding. Drugs, dental, vision and paramedical care for working-age employees mostly depend on employer plans.
benefits.cite: Health Insurance Act (ON); Medicare Protection Act (BC)

benefits.detail: Tech market norm: extended health and dental (80-100% coinsurance), vision, and paramedical/mental health (often C$1,000-2,500+). Plus life insurance (1-3x salary), AD&D, STD, LTD, EAP, virtual care, and a health or lifestyle spending account. LTD is often employee-paid so benefits are received tax-free.

Employer-paid group term life premiums and lifestyle/wellness spending accounts are taxable benefits. Employer-paid private health and dental premiums are not taxable federally, but are taxable in Quebec for provincial tax. Report taxable benefits on the T4.
benefits.cite: Income Tax Act s.6; CRA T4130 guide

benefits.detail: Group RRSP with an employer match through a DPSP (e.g., 50-100% of employee contributions up to 3-6% of salary), with DPSP vesting of at most 2 years. RRSP room is 18% of prior-year earnings up to the annual dollar limit (verify the 2026 limit). Registered pension plans are uncommon in US-owned tech.
benefits.cite: Income Tax Act s.146, s.147; market practice

benefits.detail: Register a SUB plan for parental leave top-ups. A qualifying short-term disability plan can earn a reduced employer EI premium through the EI Premium Reduction Program (verify eligibility).

In ON, employer benefit plan contributions must continue through the ESA statutory notice period. Common-law damages include benefits for the whole reasonable notice period, and LTD can be a major uninsured risk if an employee becomes disabled during that period. Check that carrier contracts allow continuation.

Forfeiture on termination must clearly and unambiguously exclude the common-law notice period, or damages may include vesting during notice (Matthews v. Ocean Nutrition, 2020 SCC 26). Make sure employees accept the grant terms (Battiston v. Microsoft, 2021 ONCA 727).
benefits.cite: Matthews v. Ocean Nutrition 2020 SCC 26; Battiston v. Microsoft 2021 ONCA 727

performanceAndConduct.detail: Poor performance rarely amounts to just cause. Dismissal with cause requires clear expectations, warnings, a real chance to improve and a proportionate response (McKinley v. BC Tel). In ON, no ESA notice or severance is owed only for 'wilful misconduct, disobedience or wilful neglect of duty', a higher bar than common-law cause.
performanceAndConduct.cite: McKinley v. BC Tel 2001 SCC 38; ON O. Reg. 288/01 s.2

performanceAndConduct.detail: ON: investigate every complaint appropriately (an inspector can order a third-party investigation at the employer's cost) and tell both parties in writing of the results and any corrective action. BC: follow written procedures with a reasonable response aimed at fully addressing the incident; keep records.
performanceAndConduct.cite: ON OHSA s.32.0.7, s.55.3; WorkSafeBC bullying and harassment policies

performanceAndConduct.detail: Accommodate disability, family status and creed to the point of undue hardship through an interactive, documented process. Complaints go to the HRTO (1-year limit) or BC Human Rights Tribunal (1 year) with uncapped general damages.
performanceAndConduct.cite: ON Human Rights Code s.11, s.17, s.34; BC Human Rights Code s.13, s.22

performanceAndConduct.detail: Follow the ON e-monitoring policy. Keep searches of devices and accounts proportionate: intrusion upon seclusion is actionable in ON (Jones v. Tsige 2012 ONCA 32), and BC PIPA requires reasonable purposes and notice. Keep an investigation protocol for insider-threat and IP cases.
performanceAndConduct.cite: ON ESA Part XI.1; BC PIPA ss.13, 16, 19

performanceAndConduct.detail: Unilateral cuts to pay or role, relocation, indefinite administrative suspension, or reversing remote status can amount to dismissal (Potter v. NB Legal Aid 2015 SCC 10). Get consent with consideration, or give working notice of the change.
performanceAndConduct.cite: Potter v. New Brunswick Legal Aid Services Commission, 2015 SCC 10

performanceAndConduct.detail: Reprisals are prohibited for ESA, OHSA and pay-transparency complaints and for pay discussions in BC. Criminal Code s.425.1 makes retaliation against employees who report offences to authorities a crime. Align the US SOX hotline with these protections.
performanceAndConduct.cite: ON ESA s.74; OHSA s.50; BC Pay Transparency Act s.4; Criminal Code s.425.1

performanceAndConduct.detail: Random testing is generally not allowed outside dangerous workplaces with evidence of a problem (Irving Pulp & Paper). Treat addiction as a disability that requires accommodation.
performanceAndConduct.cite: CEP Local 30 v. Irving Pulp & Paper, 2013 SCC 34

termination.detail: Waksdale (2020 ONCA): if any termination provision (including the for-cause clause) breaches the ESA, all of them fall. Dufault v. Ignace (2024 ONSC 1029; aff'd 2024 ONCA 915; SCC leave denied June 5, 2025) voided a clause over 'sole discretion ... at any time' wording, a cause definition and the benefits wording. In Baker v. Van Dolder's Home Team (2026 ONCA 568, Aug 2026) the ONCA held that 'at any time' and 'for any reason' are not invalid when the contract is read as a whole and repeatedly guarantees ESA minimums.
termination.cite: Waksdale v. Swegon 2020 ONCA 391; Dufault 2024 ONCA 915; Baker 2026 ONCA 568

termination.detail: Use an ESA-minimums savings clause. Define cause more broadly than 'wilful misconduct' only if ESA entitlements are expressly preserved. Continue benefits and pay all ESA amounts (notice, severance, vacation pay). Avoid 'sole discretion' wording tied to termination timing; Baker did not squarely address it. Re-paper legacy contracts with fresh consideration.

If there is no enforceable clause, notice reflects age, length of service, character of employment and availability of similar work. Inducement from secure prior jobs can lengthen it; 24 months is a soft cap except in exceptional cases. The employee must mitigate, but ESA amounts cannot be reduced by mitigation.
termination.cite: Bardal v. Globe & Mail (1960); Dawe v. Equitable Life 2019 ONCA 512

termination.detail: ON: ESA notice or pay (up to 8 weeks) plus ESA severance (up to 26 weeks) at 5+ years' service with C$2.5M+ global payroll. BC: CLOS up to 8 weeks. All must be paid in full regardless of any release.
termination.cite: ON ESA ss.54-65; BC ESA s.63

termination.detail: Without an enforceable early-termination clause, an employer ending a fixed-term contract early owes the balance of the term with no duty to mitigate (Howard v. Benson Group 2016 ONCA 256). Repeated renewals can turn the job into indefinite employment.
termination.cite: Howard v. Benson Group Inc., 2016 ONCA 256

termination.detail: ON: 50+ employees at an establishment within 4 weeks requires 8/12/16 weeks' notice (50-199 / 200-499 / 500+), a Form 1 filed with the Director and posted, plus 3 days' job-seeking leave. BC: 50+ at a single location within 2 months requires 8/12/16 weeks' notice (50-100 / 101-300 / 301+) to employees, any union and the Minister, on top of individual CLOS.
termination.cite: ON ESA s.58 and O. Reg. 288/01; BC ESA s.64

termination.detail: Common-law damages include bonuses and equity that would have been earned or vested during the notice period unless plan wording unambiguously removes them. Model the equity cost before deciding on terminations.

Dismissal linked to leave, disability, pregnancy or a complaint exposes the employer to ESA reinstatement orders, human rights damages and reprisal findings. Run a pre-termination checklist: leave status, accommodation file, recent complaints.
termination.cite: ON ESA s.74; Human Rights Codes

exit.detail: ON: all wages, termination pay and severance by the later of 7 days after termination or the next regular payday. BC: within 48 hours after the last day worked if the employer terminates, or 6 days if the employee quits. Include accrued vacation pay.
exit.cite: ON ESA s.11(5), s.65; BC ESA s.18

exit.detail: Electronic ROE due within 5 calendar days after the end of the pay period in which the interruption of earnings occurs. For monthly or 13-period payrolls, the deadline is the earlier of that date or 15 days after the interruption. Use the correct reason code; misstatement is an offence.
exit.cite: Employment Insurance Regulations s.19; Service Canada ROE guide

exit.detail: Continue benefits through the ESA notice period (ON). Communicate life and health conversion deadlines, and settle how equity and bonus are treated in writing.

Offer consideration above ESA minimums in exchange for a full and final release. Give the employee reasonable time and recommend independent legal advice. Withhold tax on retiring allowances (lump-sum rates of 10%, 20% or 30% by amount, outside Quebec).
exit.cite: Common law; Income Tax Regulations s.103

exit.req: Asset return, access and IP protection
exit.detail: Revoke access on the notice date, recover devices, remind the employee of confidentiality and invention-assignment obligations, and certify return of data. Log exits of export-controlled technology holders under the technology control plan.
exit.cite: Contract; common law breach of confidence; US EAR

exit.detail: Issue a T4 (and RL-1 for Quebec) by the end of February of the next year, including retiring allowance amounts. Keep payroll records 6 years.
exit.cite: Income Tax Regulations s.200; Income Tax Act s.230

recordsAndPrivacy.detail: PIPEDA does not cover employee data of provincially regulated Ontario employers. Rely on the common law (intrusion upon seclusion), the ESA e-monitoring policy, contracts and good practice. Apply BC PIPA-level standards company-wide for consistency.
recordsAndPrivacy.cite: PIPEDA s.4(1)(b); Jones v. Tsige 2012 ONCA 32

recordsAndPrivacy.detail: Employee personal information may be collected, used and disclosed without consent if reasonable for establishing, managing or ending employment, after notifying the employee. Designate a privacy officer and handle access requests within PIPA timelines. Storing data outside Canada is allowed with appropriate safeguards and transparency.

CRA payroll: 6 years. ON ESA employee and wage records: 3 years. ON job postings, applications and interview-outcome records: 3 years. ON policies: 3 years after replacement. BC ESA payroll: 4 years after employment ends (verify). Foreign-worker documents: 6 years. Harassment investigation files should be kept for the limitation period and any litigation hold.
recordsAndPrivacy.cite: Income Tax Act s.230; ON ESA s.15; BC ESA s.28; IRPR

recordsAndPrivacy.detail: PIPEDA requires breach reporting where there is a real risk of significant harm (commercial data). Quebec Law 25 requires breach reporting and a privacy impact assessment before transferring data outside Quebec. Tell employees that HR data is processed by the US parent and vendors.
recordsAndPrivacy.cite: PIPEDA s.10.1; Quebec Private Sector Act (Law 25)

recordsAndPrivacy.detail: Disclose AI screening in ON postings (since Jan 2026). Assess automated decision tools for human rights bias, and give privacy notices under BC PIPA or Quebec Law 25 (which requires notice of decisions based exclusively on automated processing).
recordsAndPrivacy.cite: ON ESA job posting provisions; Quebec Law 25 s.12.1

recordsAndPrivacy.detail: Bill C-27 (Consumer Privacy Protection Act and the AI and Data Act) died when Parliament was prorogued in Jan 2025. Bill C-36 (Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act), tabled June 15, 2026, proposes penalties of up to 3% of global revenue (administrative) and 5% (criminal). Its coverage of employee data mirrors PIPEDA (federally regulated only; verify).
recordsAndPrivacy.cite: Bill C-36 (45th Parliament), first reading June 15, 2026

healthSafety.detail: Written OHS policy and program reviewed annually. JHSC at 20+ workers (with certified members) or a health and safety representative at 6-19 workers. Awareness training, required postings, and WSIB-compliant first aid (Reg. 1101).
healthSafety.cite: ON OHSA ss.9, 25; O. Reg. 297/13; WSIB Reg. 1101

healthSafety.detail: Keep the policies and programs, and do a workplace violence risk assessment. Harassment includes virtual or online conduct (since Oct 28, 2024). Review annually and train workers.
healthSafety.cite: ON OHSA Part III.0.1 (Working for Workers Five Act, 2024)

healthSafety.detail: ON: report to WSIB (Form 7) within 3 business days of learning of an injury needing health care beyond first aid or causing lost time. BC: report to WorkSafeBC within 3 days. Investigate incidents and keep first-aid records.
healthSafety.cite: ON WSIA s.21; BC Workers Compensation Act

healthSafety.detail: Register with WorkSafeBC. Required: a formal OHS program at 50+ workers, a JOHSC at 20+ or worker representative at 10-19, new worker orientation, a first-aid assessment, and working-alone procedures. Bullying and harassment policies must be reviewed annually.
healthSafety.cite: BC Workers Compensation Act Part 2; OHS Regulation Parts 3-4

healthSafety.detail: For silicon validation, failure-analysis or reliability labs: WHMIS training, safety data sheet management, and designated-substance and ventilation controls. ESD, laser and high-voltage safety procedures are also expected.
healthSafety.cite: ON O. Reg. 860 (WHMIS); BC OHS Regulation Part 5; Hazardous Products Act

healthSafety.detail: ON OHSA excludes much work done in a private residence by its occupant, but virtual harassment is covered and employer duties to ask about home-work risks are expected practice. WorkSafeBC expects employers to assess home-office ergonomics and working-alone risks.
Provide individualized workplace emergency response information to employees with disabilities (AODA), and keep the evacuation plan and fire warden roles current.
healthSafety.cite: AODA O. Reg. 191/11 s.27; Ontario Fire Code

terminationDeepDive.voluntary: Neither the ON nor the BC ESA requires resignation notice. At common law an employee owes reasonable notice (usually 2-4 weeks, as set in the contract), but damage claims against departing engineers are rare and hard to prove. Resignations should be in writing and unequivocal; a heat-of-the-moment resignation may not be binding. The employer may waive the notice period, but in ON waiving it early can amount to a dismissal, so pay out the notice period (or at least the ESA-required portion) to be safe. Garden leave is only available if the contract allows it or the employee agrees, and it counts toward any notice period.
terminationDeepDive.involuntary: Termination without cause is lawful with notice: working notice, pay in lieu, or both. Pay ESA amounts plus common-law notice unless an enforceable clause limits entitlement (in ON, post-Baker 2026 ONCA 568, holistic ESA-compliant drafting still matters). Just cause is a high, proportionality-based bar (McKinley). In ON, ESA amounts are forfeited only for wilful misconduct. Deliver a written termination letter setting out final pay, benefits end date, equity treatment and ROE, and hold a short, respectful meeting (bad-faith manner risks Honda v. Keays / Wallace-type damages). Risk factors: protected leave, recent complaints, disability, and age combined with long service.
terminationDeepDive.redundancy: There is no statutory selection method or consultation duty for non-union staff. Ontario mass termination (50+ at an establishment within 4 weeks) needs 8 weeks' notice (50-199), 12 (200-499) or 16 (500+). File Form 1 with the Director of Employment Standards; notice is not effective until it is received, and it must be posted in the workplace. Employees get 3 unpaid job-seeking days during notice (since Nov 27, 2025), and ESA severance still applies. Exception: 10% or less of the workforce, not caused by a permanent closure. BC group termination (50+ at a single location within 2 months) needs 8 weeks' notice (50-100), 12 (101-300) or 16 (301+). Give it to each employee, any union and the Minister of Labour, stating the number affected, effective dates and reasons; this is in addition to individual CLOS. Common-law notice applies to every affected employee in both provinces.
terminationDeepDive.finalPayTiming: ON: final wages, vacation pay, termination pay and severance are due by the later of 7 days after employment ends or the next regular payday. Severance may be paid in instalments over up to 3 years with the employee's written agreement or Director approval. BC: within 48 hours after the last day worked if the employer terminates, and within 6 days if the employee quits. Penalties: ON notices of contravention with escalating fixed penalties, orders to pay, and prosecution (corporate fines up to C$500,000 for repeat convictions). BC administrative penalties of C$500, C$2,500 and C$10,000 per contravention, plus determinations with interest.
requiredDocuments: Written termination letter (notice or pay in lieu, ESA and contractual entitlements, benefits end date, equity and bonus treatment)
ON mass termination: Form 1 filed with the Director and posted; BC group termination: written notice to employees, union and Minister
Record of Employment (electronic, within 5 calendar days after the end of the pay period with the interruption)
Final pay statement including vacation pay
Release and settlement agreement (if enhanced package offered)
T4 (and RL-1 if Quebec) for the final year, by end of February
Reminder of continuing confidentiality, IP and non-solicit obligations; certification of return of property and data
terminationDeepDive.releaseAgreements: Releases are enforceable if supported by new consideration beyond what the employee is already owed (ESA amounts must be paid regardless and cannot be conditioned on signing). They must be clear and signed voluntarily with reasonable time to consider; no statutory review period exists, but 5-10 business days and a recommendation to get independent legal advice are standard. Courts may set aside unconscionable releases (unequal bargaining power, improvident terms). Human rights claims can be released if the release is informed and voluntary. There is no OWBPA-style age-waiver regime. In Quebec, use a French transaction under the Civil Code. Structure lump sums as retiring allowances (withholding 10%, 20% or 30% by amount) and consider EI allocation of severance.
terminationDeepDive.typicalPackage: Market practice for tech/semiconductor employers, not law: without an enforceable termination clause, opening offers are often about 3-4 weeks per year of service with a 2-3 month minimum for professionals. Settlements typically land at about 60-80% of the realistic common-law range (roughly 3-6 months for short-service engineers, 12-24 months for long-service senior leaders). They usually include benefits continuation, a pro-rated bonus, negotiated equity vesting treatment, outplacement (1-3 months) and a legal-fee contribution (C$1,000-2,500). With an enforceable ESA-minimums clause, employers commonly pay ESA amounts plus a modest enhancement (e.g., 2 weeks per year) for a release.

recentChanges.title: Ontario Court of Appeal: 'at any time' termination clauses not invalid per se
recentChanges.detail: Baker v. Van Dolder's Home Team Inc.; Li v. Wayfair Canada ULC, 2026 ONCA 568 (Aug 6, 2026). Clauses allowing termination 'at any time' or 'for any reason' are read holistically and are enforceable where the contract repeatedly guarantees ESA minimums. Cause clauses broader than wilful misconduct are acceptable if ESA entitlements are preserved. Waksdale was not revisited.

recentChanges.title: BC ESA complaint-process reforms in force
recentChanges.detail: Bill 10, the Labour Statutes Amendment Act, 2026 (royal assent Apr 16, 2026; in force Aug 1, 2026). It adds staged complaint intake and a mandatory resolution process, and requires employers to deposit the full amount owed before appealing a determination.

recentChanges.title: Federal privacy reform re-launched: Bill C-36
recentChanges.detail: Bill C-36, the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act, was tabled June 15, 2026 to replace PIPEDA's privacy provisions after Bill C-27 died in Jan 2025. It proposes administrative penalties up to the greater of C$10M or 3% of global revenue, and enforcement by a new Digital Safety and Data Protection Commission.

recentChanges.title: Ontario job-posting transparency rules in force
recentChanges.detail: For employers with 25+ employees: pay or a range in public postings (max C$50,000 spread; exempt above C$200,000), disclosure of AI in screening, a vacancy-status statement, no 'Canadian experience' requirement, a response to interviewed applicants within 45 days, and 3-year record retention.

recentChanges.title: BC pay transparency reporting expands to 50+ employees
recentChanges.detail: Employers with 50+ BC employees on Jan 1, 2026 (about 8,500 employers) must publish their first gender pay-gap report by Nov 1, 2026. The report covers hourly pay, overtime and bonus gaps for the previous calendar year. Non-compliant employers may be publicly named.

recentChanges.title: 2026 CPP/CPP2/EI parameters
recentChanges.detail: YMPE C$74,600 and YAMPE C$85,000 (CPP 5.95%, CPP2 4%). EI maximum insurable earnings C$68,900, with the employee rate cut to 1.63% (1.30% in Quebec).

recentChanges.title: Ontario Working for Workers Seven Act, 2025 (Bill 30)
recentChanges.detail: Royal assent Nov 27, 2025. Adds 3 unpaid job-seeking days during mass-termination notice periods and longer temporary layoffs by agreement with Director approval. Also OHSA administrative monetary penalties and higher WSIA penalties. Job-board fraud-reporting duties started Jan 1, 2026.

recentChanges.title: BC sick-note ban and 27-week serious illness leave
recentChanges.detail: Bill 11: from Nov 12, 2025, employers may not require medical notes for absences of up to 5 consecutive days for the first 2 absences each calendar year. Bill 30: from Nov 28, 2025, up to 27 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for serious personal illness or injury.

recentChanges.title: 2026-2028 Immigration Levels Plan (with Budget 2025)
recentChanges.detail: Temporary-worker arrival targets cut to 230,000 a year for 2026-28 (from 367,750), study permits to 155,000, and permanent residents held at 380,000. The goal is temporary residents below 5% of the population by end-2027. Budget 2025 announced an accelerated pathway for H-1B holders (not yet launched as of Sept 2026).

recentChanges.title: Ontario new-hire information statement
recentChanges.detail: Since July 1, 2025, employers with 25+ employees must give written details (employer names, contact, work location, pay, pay period and payday, anticipated hours) before the first day where practicable.

recentChanges.title: Ontario long-term illness leave (27 weeks)
recentChanges.detail: In force June 19, 2025: up to 27 weeks of unpaid leave in a 52-week period for a serious medical condition, after 13 weeks' employment, with a health practitioner certificate.

recentChanges.title: Supreme Court of Canada declines Dufault appeal
recentChanges.detail: On June 5, 2025 the SCC dismissed leave to appeal in Township of Ignace v. Dufault, leaving the ONCA decision in place (clause void over its cause definition and 'sole discretion ... at any time' wording). This fuelled lower-court splits until Baker (Aug 2026).

recentChanges.title: Competition Act: private enforcement opens
recentChanges.detail: From June 20, 2025, private parties can go to the Competition Tribunal (with leave) under abuse of dominance and s.90.1. Since Dec 15, 2024, s.90.1 also reaches anti-competitive agreements between non-competitors. This adds to the criminal wage-fixing and no-poach offence in force since June 23, 2023.

recentChanges.title: Spousal open work permits restricted
recentChanges.detail: From Jan 21, 2025, spouses qualify only if the principal worker is in a TEER 0/1 (or listed TEER 2/3) job with 16+ months remaining on the permit. Dependent children no longer qualify. This affects relocation packages for mid-level engineers.

recentChanges.title: Ontario Working for Workers Five Act, 2024 (Bill 190) in force
recentChanges.detail: From Oct 28, 2024: employers cannot require medical notes for the 3 ESA sick days; OHSA harassment explicitly includes virtual or online harassment; OHSA documents may be posted electronically. It also set the stage for the 2026 job-posting duties (vacancy disclosure, 45-day response).

watchlist.title: Further appeals on termination clauses
watchlist.detail: Watch for an SCC leave application in Baker/Li (2026 ONCA 568) and for how courts treat 'sole discretion' wording after Baker. Re-paper Ontario contracts once the position settles.

watchlist.title: Bill C-36 (Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act)
watchlist.detail: Replacement for PIPEDA's privacy provisions with stronger penalties and a new commission. Commencement depends on Bill C-34. Monitor for committee amendments affecting HR data and AI.

watchlist.title: H-1B and Express Entry category changes
watchlist.detail: IRCC consulted from Aug 4 to Sept 1, 2026 on new category-based selection priorities for H-1B holders (STEM), researchers, Global Talent Stream workers and International Talent Attraction Strategy participants. These could create a recruiting channel from US H-1B engineers.

watchlist.title: Ontario placement-of-child leave and the next Working for Workers bill
watchlist.detail: The 16-week unpaid adoption/surrogacy placement leave (Working for Workers Six Act) awaits proclamation. Ontario has introduced a Working for Workers bill every year since 2021.
watchlist.expected: Proclamation TBD; next bill likely fall 2026 or spring 2027

watchlist.title: Competition Bureau anti-competitive conduct guidelines
watchlist.detail: Draft guidelines (released Oct 31, 2025; comments closed Jan 29, 2026) will be finalized. Watch for any labour-market or non-compete content, and for the first private-access cases involving employment restraints.

watchlist.title: BC pay transparency next phase
watchlist.detail: An extension to all employers and possible penalties are discussed but not implemented. The first 50+ employee reports (Nov 2026) will attract public scrutiny of pay gaps.

watchlist.title: Temporary resident reductions and LMIA policy
watchlist.detail: Continued tightening under the 2026-2028 levels plan. Watch Global Talent Stream occupation list updates, LMIA wage thresholds and any Bill 30-style provincial immigration changes affecting OINP and BC PNP tech draws.

calendar.title: Jan 1 headcount snapshot and rate changes
calendar.detail: Count ON employees: 25+ triggers the disconnecting and e-monitoring policies (due Mar 1) plus the job-posting and new-hire information rules. Count BC employees for pay transparency reporting (as at Jan 1). New CPP/CPP2/EI and tax tables apply to the first payroll.

calendar.title: Annual review of harassment, violence and OHS policies
calendar.detail: ON OHSA requires violence/harassment policies and the OHS policy to be reviewed at least annually. WorkSafeBC expects an annual review of bullying and harassment policies and procedures. Record the review date.

calendar.title: Recurring: ROE deadlines (every pay period)
calendar.detail: Electronic ROE within 5 calendar days after the end of the pay period with an interruption of earnings (leave, termination, layoff). Monthly payrolls: the earlier of that date or 15 days after the interruption.

calendar.title: T4/T4A slips and summary due
calendar.detail: File with the CRA and give to employees by the last day of February (the next business day if it falls on a weekend). Electronic filing is required above 5 slips. RL-1 slips for Quebec employees. Family Day falls on the 3rd Monday (ON and BC).

calendar.title: Ontario policy deadline: March 1
calendar.detail: Disconnecting-from-work and electronic-monitoring policies must be in place if there were 25+ ON employees on Jan 1. Distribute within 30 days and keep for 3 years.

calendar.title: RRSP contribution deadline
calendar.detail: The deadline for prior-year RRSP deductions is the 60th day of the year (about Mar 1-2). Ensure group RRSP and DPSP contributions are remitted and year-end matching is trued up.

calendar.title: BC minimum wage adjustment and T2/SR&ED timing
calendar.detail: BC minimum wage changes June 1 (C$18.25 in 2026). For a Dec 31 year-end, the T2 is due June 30. The SR&ED claim (T661) is due 18 months after the tax year-end, so gather engineering time records now.

calendar.title: National Day for Truth and Reconciliation (Sept 30)
calendar.detail: Statutory holiday in BC (not in ON for provincially regulated employers). Plan coverage and communications. Labour Day falls on the 1st Monday.

calendar.title: Ontario minimum wage adjustment
calendar.detail: ON minimum wage rises Oct 1 (to C$17.95 in 2026; student C$16.90). Update intern and co-op rates and pay-range floors. Thanksgiving is the 2nd Monday (ON and BC).

calendar.title: BC Pay Transparency Report due Nov 1
calendar.detail: Employers with 50+ BC employees (from 2026) publish the report on their website or in the workplace by Nov 1, using prior-calendar-year data. Remembrance Day (Nov 11) is a BC statutory holiday.

calendar.title: AODA accessibility compliance report (Dec 31, 2026)
calendar.detail: Private-sector organizations with 20+ ON employees file the online compliance report every 3 years (next after 2026: 2029). Also refresh the multi-year accessibility plan and confirm AODA training records.

calendar.title: Year-end payroll and poster checks
calendar.detail: Reconcile taxable benefits and equity income for T4s. Confirm the ESA poster version (ON) and required OHSA postings. Review vacation carryover under the ON 10-month and BC 12-month taking rules. Plan Jan 1 policy updates for the Working for Workers changes.

gotchas: Using a US at-will offer letter, or none: without an enforceable termination clause, a mid-level engineer can claim 3-12+ months of common-law notice. In Ontario, one non-compliant sentence (often the for-cause clause) voids the whole clause (Waksdale).

Rolling out a new contract after the start date without new consideration: termination, IP and restrictive-covenant terms signed on day 10 are unenforceable. Send contracts with the offer and get them signed before start.

Copying US equity grant language: forfeiture on 'termination date' without expressly excluding the common-law notice period lets departing employees claim RSUs that would have vested during notice (Matthews v. Ocean Nutrition 2020 SCC 26).
Forgetting Ontario ESA severance: the C$2.5M payroll test uses global payroll, so every Ontario employee with 5+ years' service is owed up to 26 weeks on top of notice.

Importing US non-competes: they are void for Ontario employees below the C-suite (ESA s.67.2) and rarely enforceable in BC. Rely on confidentiality, IP assignment, narrow non-solicits and notice-period garden leave.

Global ATS templates that ask for salary history (illegal for BC applicants), omit pay ranges (BC; Ontario at 25+ employees), use ranges wider than C$50,000 or fail to disclose AI screening (Ontario 2026), or never close the loop with interviewed Ontario candidates within 45 days.

Running a US WARN-style RIF plan: Ontario needs 8-16 weeks' mass notice plus a Form 1 to the Director before notice takes effect. BC group notice is added on top of individual CLOS, and common-law notice still applies to every employee.

Assuming PIPEDA covers Ontario employee data (it doesn't) or that no rules apply: the e-monitoring policy, intrusion upon seclusion and BC PIPA still constrain monitoring, and Quebec Law 25 applies to any Quebec remote employee.

Letting managers hire remote staff in Quebec without setup: French contracts and policies, OQLF registration at 25+ employees, a psychological harassment policy, QPP/QPIP payroll and a reinstatement right after 2 years' service.

Engaging long-term Canadian 'contractors' who work like employees: CRA can assess CPP/EI, ESA claims follow, and Ontario courts award reasonable notice even to dependent contractors (Keenan v. Canac Kitchens 2016 ONCA 79).
semiconductorNotes: IP and invention assignment: Canada has no statutory employee-invention regime. Unless an employee was hired to invent, courts may find the employee owns a patentable invention, so use an express present-tense assignment, a disclosure obligation and a prior-inventions schedule, signed before start. Copyright in code and designs made in the course of employment belongs to the employer (Copyright Act s.13(3)). Moral rights cannot be assigned, only waived (s.14.1), so include a written moral-rights waiver.

Trade secret protection without non-competes (Ontario ban): combine confidentiality agreements, 12-month narrowly drafted non-solicits of customers and employees, and working notice or garden leave during the notice period. Add fiduciary obligations for senior technical leaders, access controls and exit certifications. Canada has no federal civil trade-secret statute; enforcement relies on breach of confidence, contract and injunctions. Criminal Code s.391 (added 2020) criminalizes obtaining or disclosing trade secrets by deceit or fraud.

US export controls: releasing EAR-controlled chip design technology, source code or tools (e.g., advanced computing and semiconductor manufacturing items) to a third-country national in a Canadian office is a 'deemed reexport'. BIS uses the person's most recent citizenship or permanent residency, so a PRC national in Toronto may need a licence even if the item needs none for Canada. Run a technology control plan and screen before access, and apply citizenship-based restrictions only where legally required. Ontario's Code protects 'citizenship' and both provinces protect 'place of origin'. ITAR or defence items also trigger Canada's Controlled Goods Program (registration and security assessments).

Cross-border US-Canada staff: a Canadian employee working remotely from the US (or a US employee relocating to Canada) triggers payroll registration, tax withholding in the work location, CPP/EI or FICA coverage and permanent-establishment risk. Use the Canada-US totalization agreement's certificates of coverage for temporary assignments, and Regulation 102 waivers or Non-Resident Employer Certification for US employees on short Canadian business trips. Canadians taking US roles typically use TN (CUSMA) or L-1 status.

SR&ED tax credits: a subsidiary of a US-listed parent is not a CCPC. It generally gets the 15% non-refundable federal investment tax credit (not the 35% refundable enhanced rate), plus Ontario and BC provincial R&D credits (verify current rates and Budget 2025 changes to expenditure limits). The CRA expects contemporaneous evidence: project-level timesheets for engineers, technical uncertainties, hypotheses, test results and design iterations. Build SR&ED time coding into engineering time tracking and file the T661 within 18 months of year-end.

Talent routes for chip design hires: the Global Talent Stream (10-business-day LMIA standard, 2-week work permit) covers software and computer engineers (confirm electrical/electronics engineer eligibility on the current list). Intra-company transfers work well for moving US or Asian engineers into Toronto or Vancouver. Spousal work permit limits since Jan 2025 mean checking the TEER 0/1 classification of the principal's role before relocation.

Research security: university collaborations (NSERC Alliance, Mitacs interns) involving semiconductors or other sensitive technology research areas are subject to the federal Policy on Sensitive Technology Research and Affiliations of Concern (named research organizations list). Screen academic partners and interns accordingly. Investment Canada Act national-security reviews apply to acquisitions of Canadian chip companies.

Semiconductor equity-heavy pay: RSUs are taxed at vesting and the stock option deduction is capped at C$200,000 per vesting year for large non-CCPC employers. Equity makes up much of common-law notice damages for senior engineers, so draft plan forfeiture terms to Matthews standards and model equity exposure before reductions in force.
